title: Psalms for the sick
hook: communities divide the whole book to read for someone who is ill

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one twenty-six, the song before grace. Your line was sow in tears, reap in joy. Did you do one hard thing whose fruit you can't see yet? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

The news comes into the group chat late at night. Someone's mother is in the hospital. It's serious. And within an hour, something happens that's become common in Jewish communities: a list appears. Psalms one to ten, Sarah. Eleven to twenty, David. Twenty-one to thirty, the Cohens. By the next evening, a whole community of people, some of whom have never met the sick woman, has read the entire Book of Psalms for her. Today: psalms for the sick.
screen: `A MESSAGE LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A LIST APPEARS.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK, FOR ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Saying psalms for someone who is ill is one of the oldest and most widespread Jewish customs. When there's nothing else to do, you can do this. Often it's shared: a group divides all one hundred fifty psalms, so the whole book gets said for one person, sometimes every day. The person is named in the Hebrew way, with their own name and their mother's: Sarah, daughter of Rachel. Some add a custom with the longest psalm, one nineteen, which is arranged by the Hebrew alphabet: they read the sections whose letters spell the sick person's name. Some psalms are especially loved for this. Psalm twenty: "The LORD answer thee in the day of trouble". Psalm thirty, a song of someone who cried out and was healed. And the prayer for healing goes back to the Torah itself. When Moses' sister Miriam became ill, Moses cried out five short words in Hebrew, one of the shortest prayers in the Bible: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." No long speech. Just her, and now. Jews also say a prayer called Mi she-berakh for the sick when the Torah is read, and wish each other refuah shlemah, a complete healing, of body and spirit. The psalms don't replace doctors. Jewish tradition values medicine deeply. And the Talmud teaches that visiting the sick is itself a kind of healing. But when you're far away, or it's three in the morning, or there's nothing left to try, a psalm is something you can hold, together.
screen: `A COMMUNITY DIVIDES THE BOOK.` · `NAMED WITH THEIR MOTHER'S NAME.` · `HEAL HER NOW: FIVE WORDS.` · `REFUAH SHLEMAH.` · then, large: `PSALMS FOR THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a psalm for someone who is ill. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is sick right now, in body or in spirit. Picture their face. Say their name, quietly. If you can, find Psalm twenty or Psalm thirty and read it for them. If not, use Moses' five words: heal her now, or heal him now. Or just hold them in your mind with a wish for a complete healing. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Psalms for the sick. Communities divide the whole Book of Psalms to read for someone who is ill, and wish them refuah shlemah, a complete healing.
Your line: psalms for the sick. Today, reach out to one person who's unwell. A message, a visit, a psalm said for them. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Jewish communities organize Tehillim groups that divide the Book of Psalms for someone who is ill, name them in the Mi she-berakh prayer at the Torah reading, and wish them refuah shlemah.

what it means: a community holding one sick person together, psalm by psalm, name by name.
what a scholar hears: Moses' prayer in Numbers 12:13 is five Hebrew words (El na refa na lah), and the Talmud (Nedarim 39b–40a) treats visiting the sick as part of healing.
